newsitem.title: GERMANY: German troops fight to block new tear in Oder dike.
newsitem.headline: German troops fight to block new tear in Oder dike.

text.p: Thousands of German soldiers fought on Thursday to prevent a damaged dike on the River Oder bursting open and flooding homes and crops as a new tear opened in the barrier's foundations.

The Brandenburg state interior ministry said the new damage was about 100 metres (yards) south of a gap that opened on Wednesday near the village of Hohenwutzen which soldiers were still battling to stabilise.
It was raining continuously in the area. Military helicopters were dumping sandbags onto both sections from the air and 5,000 soldiers were toiling to repair the damage.
Experts were at the scene of the new 15-metre tear, checking the extent of the damage. They could not confirm reports that water was sloshing over the dike at the new weak spot.

Around 10,000 residents of the Oder valley region on Germany's border with Poland were evacuated late on Wednesday, after the dike at Hohenwutzen threatened to give way completely under the weight of two weeks of floods. Just under 5,000 people were evacuated from the region last week.

Some of the worst floods this century have hit neighbouring Poland and the Czech Republic this month, claiming more than 100 lives. No deaths have been reported in Germany but homes, businesses and farms have been extensively damaged.

Despite the work of the troops to plug the dike with gravel and sand, the Brandenburg interior ministry thought the chances it would hold were no better than 50-50, and state Environment Minister Matthias Platzeck was even less optimistic.
"The chance that it will hold are around 10 percent," he said. "In any event we will have to work on it for the next 24 hours."
In the villages below the dike, families had packed what they could carry in their cars and left their homes, not knowing when they would return.
Farmers gathered cattle, pigs and sheep to be transported out of the region.

The Oderbruch region, once the bread basket of the former communist East Germany, was drained 250 years ago by King Frederick the Great of Prussia to create fertile farmland. It is vulnerable to flooding because it lies lower than the river, which is held back by dikes.
Brandenburg Premier Manfred Stolpe estimated the damage so far at around one billion marks ($550 million).
On Wednesday the European Union proposed to provide 1.5 million Ecus ($1.6 million) in relief aid for Brandenburg.

Most of the damage is south of Frankfurt an der Oder, some 70 km (45 miles) east of Berlin, where the dike burst in several places last week. In the villages of Wiesenau and Ziltendorf more than 100 homes are still under water.
Officials were due to begin inoculations this week to prevent any diseases from the rotting carcasses of drowned animals.
